newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea suspects Northern agents killed civilians.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea suspects Northern agents killed civilians.

text.p: South Korean troops found the bodies of three civilians, one an elderly woman who had been battered and suffocated, on Wednesday and the defence ministry said it suspected North Korean infiltrators were responsible.
The brutal murders were certain to add fuel to a crisis on the Korean peninsula sparked by the intrusion of 26 North Koreans aboard a submarine last month.
Adding to the tension was an announcement that South Korea and the United States would this month start annual war games involving a U.S. aircraft carrier.
The bodies were found covered with grass on an east coast mountain near where the North Korean agents landed last month.
The 67-year-old woman had been bludgeoned with a heavy implement before being suffocated, the defence ministry said in a statement. Two men, aged 54 and 45, had been shot.
Empty M-16 rifle cartridges were found next to the bodies.
The local men were reported missing on Tuesday after they failed to return from picking mushrooms. A search was launched after residents reported hearing two gunshots.
"We suspect the remnants of the North Korean infiltrators were responsible," a ministry statement said.

Of the 26 North Koreans who came ashore on a beach near the east coast city of Kangnung, 22 were killed by Southern troops or found dead, one has been captured and a hunt is under way for the other three.
The U.S.-led United Nations Command in Seoul said annual military exercises, codenamed Foal Eagle '96, would be conducted from October 28 to November 10.
The carrier Independence and the majority of South Korean and U.S. troops stationed in South Korea will participate in the drill.
The United States stations 37,000 servicemen in South Korea to support the 655,000-strong South Korean military against any attack from the communist North.
The U.N. Command overseas a fragile ceasefire that has kept the peace on the peninsula since the 1950-53 Korean War.
North Korea denounces Foal Eagle as being preparation for an invasion of the North.
Pyongyang has threatened "merciless retaliation" for the deaths of its soldiers and has demanded Seoul return the submarine along with the survivors and bodies of the dead crew.
Seoul has warned that any provocation will meet "stern punishment" and has bolstered security at airports, ports, diplomatic missions and five west coast islands most vulnerable to a northern attack.

Pyongyang's charge on Sunday that it had seized a U.S. citizen spying for Seoul has added further fuel to the fire. Seoul said the North fabricated the charge and said the man was a 22-year missionary based in northeast China.
Winston Lord, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for East Asia and Pacific Affairs, is due to arrive in Seoul on Thursday on a three-day visit to discuss the crisis.
